# Results — Study 268 (Sahm-Rule) on BLS unemployment + the S&P 500

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The U-3 seasonally-adjusted
unemployment rate (BLS `LNS14000000`, 1959-2025) is hardcoded in
[`data.py`](../sahm_rule/data.py). The S&P 500 daily close (price-only) is from the
repo-level cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`). Match the fingerprints below
to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| BLS U-3 unemployment (SA, monthly) | 1959-01 … 2025-12 | 804 months | `061549f98555` |
| S&P 500 (^GSPC) daily close (price-only) | 1959-01 … 2025-12 | 16,863 days | `39484c0862b4` |

## The trigger

The Sahm Rule fires when the 3-month-average SA unemployment rate rises ≥ 0.50pp
above its trailing-12-month minimum. On this table there are **12 distinct onsets**:

    1959-11, 1960-10, 1970-03, 1974-07, 1980-02, 1981-11,
    1990-10, 2001-07, 2003-08, 2008-02, 2020-04, 2024-07

These line up with every postwar recession (plus a couple of mid-cycle false
alarms, e.g. 2003 and 2024) — confirming the rule is an excellent recession
*identifier*. The question is whether it is a *sell button*.

## Event study — forward S&P returns after a trigger (1-month execution lag)

The unemployment print for month *m* is released in *m+1*; we act at the close of
*m+1* (one-month execution lag) and measure the forward 12-month **price** return.
The honest baseline is the **unconditional** 12-month forward return (equities
drift up; a sell signal must beat staying invested, not beat zero).

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| n events | 12 |
| Mean 12m return **after a trigger** | **+11.9%** |
| Unconditional mean 12m return | **+8.6%** |
| Difference (event − baseline) | **+3.4pp** (wrong sign for a sell signal) |
| Welch t (event vs all months) | **+0.516** (p = 0.616) |
| HAC / Newey-West t (event fwd − baseline vs 0) | **+0.55** |
| Block-permutation p (one-sided: trigger → low) | **0.765** |

The post-trigger return is **higher** than average. The two genuine losers (2001:
−19%, 2008: −40%) are outweighed by recovery-year winners (1970: +28%, 1980: +33%,
2020: +38%). The trigger fires *after* the decline is largely priced; the forward
year is often the rebound.

## Horizon robustness

| Horizon | Event mean | Unconditional | Diff | Welch t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 6 months | +7.2% | +4.2% | +3.0pp | +0.82 |
| 12 months | +11.9% | +8.6% | +3.4pp | +0.52 |
| 24 months | +20.1% | +17.8% | +2.3pp | +0.41 |

At every horizon the post-trigger return is **at or above** baseline — the
lateness is robust, not a window artifact.

## Could you trade it? — the timing overlay

Rule: go to cash for 12 months on each trigger (1-month lag), else long the S&P;
10bps one-way per switch, on NAV (price-only).

| Strategy | CAGR | Vol | Sharpe | Max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Sahm overlay (out 12m) | **+6.5%** | 12.7% | 0.56 | **−38.5%** |
| Buy-and-hold S&P | **+7.5%** | 14.8% | 0.56 | **−52.6%** |

The overlay does cut the worst drawdown (−52.6% → −38.5%, mostly by dodging part
of 2008) **but at a 1.0pp/yr CAGR cost**, and the Sharpe ratios are identical. The
active return (overlay − B&H) has a HAC t of **−1.01** — if anything negative, and
nowhere near a positive edge. 23 switches across 65 years.

## The n = 12 problem

With only 12 triggers and ~20% annual vol on forward returns, the minimum
detectable mean shift at 80% power (two-sided, α = 0.05) is roughly:

    MDE ≈ (t_crit + t_power) * 0.20 / sqrt(12) ≈ 16pp per event

The observed gap is +3.4pp and points the *wrong way*. n = 12 cannot resolve a
real macro-timing edge even if one existed.

## Positive control

A synthetic unemployment path with **no** planted shock produces **0** triggers;
a path with a planted +3pp recession shock produces **exactly 1** trigger at the
right time. The detector is truthful — the "no sell signal" verdict is a statement
about the **market** (equities lead, unemployment lags), not a bug in the machinery.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Post-trigger 12m return +11.9% vs +8.6% unconditional; Welch
  t = +0.52, HAC t = +0.55, perm p = 0.77. No evidence the trigger precedes *low*
  returns — the sign is positive (it precedes the recovery).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The timing overlay lowers drawdown but also lowers
  CAGR, with identical Sharpe and a negative active-return t-stat. There is no
  usable sell button.
- **Busted — as a market signal.** The Sahm Rule remains a first-rate recession
  *identifier*; it is simply the wrong instrument for timing equities. Stocks lead
  the cycle; unemployment lags it.

### Honesty ledger

- **Execution lag:** +1 month beyond the reporting lag (act on the *m* print at the
  *m+1* close). Drawdowns measured forward from entry.
- **Costs:** 10bps one-way per switch on NAV. (The overlay is long/flat, no shorts,
  so no borrow.)
- **Price-only, not total return:** ^GSPC close, no dividends — this *understates*
  buy-and-hold, making the overlay look better than it is. The overlay still loses.
- **Survivorship / vintage:** the unemployment table is the *final* BLS print, not
  the real-time vintage; real-time data would trigger slightly later and revise,
  weakening the signal further. Named here on the Signal axis.
